title: Saint Etienne's Farewell
summary: Sarah Cracknell reflects on Saint Etienne's history, their final album International and returning to Melbourne for a farewell performance. She also discusses the band's surprise at learning how their music helped Winona Ryder during a difficult film shoot.
transcript:
Sarah Cracknell joins Lauren Taylor on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, to discuss Saint Etienne's farewell, 13 August 2026.

after more than three decades of their pop brilliance and 13 albums, the band are preparing to say goodbye, announcing their final album, which they put out last year, called International, which featured a bunch of collaborations on that record, including the Chemical Brothers, Paul Hartnoll from Orbital, and Australia's very own Confidence Man as well.

You may recall kind of a funny story, and it was a very sweet video that was doing the rounds on socials earlier this year of Winona Ryder, who told Elle magazine that she randomly sort of bought a Saint Etienne record from a street vendor in Lisbon at the age of 20 when she was filming and going through quite a hard time and not knowing who the band were. But she mentioned that they totally rescued her and, yeah, years later was sort of wondering if the band Saint Etienne was still together. And Saint Etienne replied to Winona Ryder that stranger things have happened, but we're glad we were there for you. And yes, we're still together.

I began my chat with Sarah Cracknell from Saint Etienne, reflecting on what it was like to find out that the band had such a strong impact on Winona Ryder.

Well, we've dined out on that a lot, obviously. It's Winona Ryder, for flip's sake. We all love Winona Ryder. She's exceptional. Love her. And even though she's shoplifted, yeah, no, I think I did that in a sweet shop once when I was about 11. So we've all been there. Actually, I don't even know if she was done for that. So jury's out. But yeah, no, that was amazing. I love that. We get lots of people saying that, you know, especially people like, you know, I went to university and was introduced to your music and it helped me in a difficult time, whatever that was, whether it was settling into uni or whether it was, I don't know, something had happened to them. But it's really nice to be so useful, you know, it's nice that we can make a difference to some people.

Do moments like that make you think about the impact your music has for people and ultimately like what the songs are about?

Very much so, yeah. Yeah, I mean, I've had, we had a song way, way back when called Archway People and people moved to Archway, which at that point in time was a little bit sketchy.

[Unclear audio at 00:02:28–00:02:30]

And I felt really guilty because these people are sort of like, I've moved to Archway from beautiful Italy. And you think, oh, no, don't do that. I mean, it's lovely now, Archway, it's been all gentrified. But so, yeah, I think the things that you say in a band, you do have to have a certain amount of responsibility for what you say.

Sarah, you called this the goodbye tour for Saint Etienne and a happy-sad thing, more of a celebration and not a wake. But how is the band sort of feeling heading into them?

Yeah, no, it's definitely more of a celebration. It's definitely that we wanted to go out on a high. I just, I wanted to leave the sort of Saint Etienne legacy intact. I mean, there's a couple of embarrassing moments, but not that many, but there could be more if we carried on, you know what I mean? There's a time, I think, when you have to just call it a day. And this is that time. But we wanted to go out and say a very sort of grateful and thankful goodbye to all our fans that we've had over the years. So, yeah, it is a celebration.

But I don't know how I'm going to feel, you know, the very last gig, because we're doing a couple of festivals. We're doing some gigs with Belle and Sebastian here. Then we're doing a tour here in September. And then we're coming to you guys in New Zealand and Australia. And then next year we'll do some more festivals, possibly a bit of Europe. But I think by the end of next year, yeah, that's it.

So when it comes to the very sort of last gig, we're quite... Especially me and Pete. Actually, Pete is the biggest crier in the band and I'm next on the list. And Bob isn't heartless. He just doesn't cry as much as we do. But I can feel, yeah, it's going to be really emotional. It is emotional already, to be honest, but it's going to get worse.

How did those conversations, the decision to wrap things up, how did they unfold? Like, who was the first to sort of go, hey, it's time?

There's a dispute about that. I think it was me. Bob thinks it might have been him. And Pete just says, well, it definitely wasn't me. I don't know. We've always been very connected in that we make records when we feel it's the right time. We make records when we all get itchy feet and think, oh, it would really be good to go back in the studio for a bit and write some songs or record some songs. So we've always been quite intuitive like that between the three of us, a bit witchy. And I think it's just the right time. It's just the right time.

Sarah, to rewind back 35 years ago now, I guess for those who may not know, Pete and Bob originally started the band as a duo and you joined as a permanent member sort of slightly later. Can you tell me and listeners the story of how you met [Unclear audio at 00:05:19–00:05:26] and what you were up to in particular just before you joined the band?

I'd had my own band since I was about 15 and we never got a deal, basically. We kind of put out a single and 12-inch ourselves and stuff. And so I thought, this isn't really going anywhere. And it's hard. It's really hard to get a deal. It's really hard. Even then, I mean, it's even harder now, I think, to be honest. And so I went to drama school because originally when I was a little kid, I wanted to be an actress, you know, I wanted to be Glenda Jackson or someone like that, a serious actress. And so I'd done that and I was doing some sort of worthy fringe plays around London. And then, of course, you know, Bob and Pete got in touch with me just at the point where I thought I'm not going to be in a band anymore. And, yeah, that's what happened.

And they came around for dinner and I basically went in to sing one song first, I guess, to see how it went. So I went in and I sang Nothing Can Stop Us, which was the first single that came out with me on it. And we just really gelled because I think we had very similar reference points growing up. We liked the same films. We liked the same TV programmes, the same music, same bands. We liked vintage clothes. I don't know. It's just, it's almost like I'd found my home, you know, band-wise. It really did feel like that.

And when you look back on those early days of Saint Etienne, what do you remember? Like have the dynamics like changed in terms of the way that you worked together since then?

Oh, definitely. So when I first joined, I didn't really do any writing with that, although I knew how to write. I'd written songs for my previous bands. But they got so many ideas already formulated in their back pockets, I'd say. So it took a little while for me to get involved in the writing. And I didn't want to come in all pushy. I'm not that kind of person. I'm just not a pushy person. I'm a very laid-back person. So very gradually, I'd start adding bits or changing lyrics so they'd flow better when I was singing. And then, yeah, it was a really gradual progression.

And now we write, all three of us. It's very... And there's no egos about songwriting. We're very glad to have someone chip in and help out when you get stuck on like, what, a third verse? I've got to write a third verse? You're kidding. I've already said everything I need to say. And so we'll chip in and help each other out. So, yeah, it's a very organic process now, writing.

You were saying your sort of connection was almost witchy and spiritual. You all seem like really great friends, the three of you. Is there particularly a secret to the band's longevity, do you think, after all these years?

I think, A, there's no egos and we're very happy to share. And I think it's quite difficult for bands that, you know, there's one key songwriter or two and they don't let the rest of the band in, you know, because it's frustrating because you come up with ideas all the time songwriting-wise and production-wise. So if you're stuck in a situation in a band where that's not happening, you're going to get fed up. And that's sometimes, I think, why bands split up.

We get on really well. We laugh all the time. I think the other reason we've been together for so long is because we haven't done lots of that, you know, those massive year-long tours and stuff like that. I mean, that's really going to be challenging for people getting on for that period of time, all exhausted and like, yeah, so we don't do that. So that probably helps the situation.

You mentioned originally wanting to be an actress before, yeah, I guess outside of music, you trained at drama school and your dad, I understand, was Stanley Kubrick's first assistant director, which is pretty amazing. Are there ways that that background shapes how you approach, I guess, a song as a performer as well?

Yeah, I think definitely in sort of lyric writing, all three of us actually, we write quite... It's quite cinematic, actually, and music sometimes, but it's quite... We sort of write songs about characters that aren't... You know, it's not autobiographical stuff. Yeah, characters in a scenario and you can leave a lot up to the imagination of the listener then, because they can fill in the gaps themselves, which is great.

And I think growing up with my dad, who worked so hard and the film industry, especially then, it was tough, you know, lots of being away from home for months on end. But I was lucky enough to go away with my dad quite a bit when I was really young, you know. And just to see that, that's going to sound really naff, but there's a sort of work ethic. It's like, you know, everyone having a super objective and that is to get the job done and get something amazing at the end of it. So I think I'm quite like that. I've got a good work ethic.

Speaking of acting too, I guess Saint Etienne famously made like a trio of films about London with director Paul Kelly. You sort of just touched on it before, but what would you say the band's relationship to cinema is?

Well, it's really strong, clearly from what you're saying, you know, three films in. As a band, we're not just about the music. We like the whole aesthetic. So for instance, all our, you know, sleeve design, we do everything. We're hands-on with that. Paul Kelly's done a lot of those sleeves, actually. So we're very in tune with him and we've worked so much with him over the years. He's done like pop videos and the films and sleeve design. So, yeah, we're about the whole package. We don't just want to, I always translate it to like, we don't want to just make a wonderful sponge cake, you know, vanilla with some cream and stuff in the middle and leave someone else to ice it. It's like, we want to be in control of the whole way it's presented and the way it looks as well as what's inside.

[Unclear audio at 00:11:29–00:15:40]

Sarah, I did want to talk to you about your latest record too. There's a strong Australian connection on the new album, Brand New Me, a collaboration with Confidence Man, which started as, I think, a song they wanted you on, but ended up as yours instead. Is that right? How did it come together?

Yeah, that's right. So they got in touch with me via Danny at Heavenly Records, saying, would I like to come and sing on something with them? So we started collaborating on Brand New Me and then they kind of really took off here and I think they just got really busy, basically. And so it kind of went on the back burner for a bit. And then when we were doing this album, International, I thought, oh, that would be good on this. Because International is such a, like we were saying, a really sort of celebratory, fun, uptempo, party vibe, and I thought Brand New Me would fit perfectly on it. So yeah, I went to them and said, is that right? And they're like, of course.

You said Confidence Man left your jaw on the floor when you saw them live. Can you tell me more about, yeah, the effect they have on you? What is it about their songs and performances?

I think, well, it's everything, but the performances are mind-blowing, aren't they? They're so good. I've seen them a few times. I think the biggest one where it really was jaw-dropping was at the Brixton Academy in London. I was on the kind of balcony bit and everyone on the balcony was jumping up and down. And I was suddenly really concerned the whole thing was going to collapse. I was like, oh my God, I'm going to die.

[Unclear audio at 00:17:47–00:17:48]

But everywhere in Brixton Academy was just going crazy. They're so brilliant. Everyone should go and see them, everybody.

You touched on this just a little bit before. Yeah, the album you made, International, being joyful and loud right after, yeah, The Night, which was more sort of quiet and ambient. Can you tell me about the relationship between those two records? And I guess did choosing like the loud, energetic record as the last one feel like the right way to say goodbye?

Yeah, it is the way to say goodbye. It almost feels like a full circle for me, or half circle, semi-circle, or like bookends. Because the first record, Foxbase Alpha, was quite eclectic and lots of ideas. You know, if you listen to it, you might go, it's not cohesive. But it is. It was like a melting pot. I think that's what I'm getting to. It's like a melting pot of ideas. And I think International is like that as well, especially because we've had so many collaborations on it, you know, with the Chemical Brothers and Erol Alkan and various. So it felt very full... Half circle to me.

You mentioned, yeah, that collaboration with Erol Alkan there and producer as well, Paul Hartnoll from Orbital. you worked with on the record too. And you mentioned they both sort of brought ideas that just fit together. You've said it felt spooky as well. Did it feel like there was a sense of destiny around that record?

Yeah. Yeah. Definitely. It was serendipitous, if that's the right word. Everyone we approached seemed to, well, they all said, that's interesting, you know, you've approached me because I actually have this track that I'm working on or that I did a little while ago. Like when I spoke to Tom from the Chemical Brothers, he's like, well, I've been working on this track with Jez from Doves, who I know as well. And he said, we kept saying in the studio, this sounds like a Saint Etienne track. It's like, send it over, you know. And so he sent it over and we were just so excited. And it was, yeah, everything fell into place. Again, witchy. We're a witchy, spooky band, I think.

Well, we're very excited to have Saint Etienne back in Australia and in Melbourne, even though it is for the very last time, a bittersweet tour, this one. You first played here, as you mentioned, at the top in Melbourne in 1998 at the Hi-Fi bar, which is now called Max Watts. Can you tell us a bit about that first time in the country, maybe places that stood out to you?

I think, I mean, it's the first and only time I've been to Australia. So, and it was part of, we'd come from somewhere else, I think. I can't remember, maybe America or something. So we were quite out of it, like, exhausted, you know, lots of flying and we were tired anyway from doing some gigs. And seeing things, I mean, it's really obvious, but seeing things like Sydney Harbour and Sydney Opera House was like, oh my God. Melbourne, we were, we kind of were a bit more chilled in Melbourne. We're like, okay, we're here. It's like, you know, really good. I remember we were very food-based in that we were so tired. We were trying to find things we could eat that pepped us up and made us feel like we had more energy. So what are they called? Moreton Bay bugs.

Oh, yeah.

We were eating those a lot, even though they look like some terrifying prehistoric or like Egyptian, what those things called in Egypt, those beetles, scarab beetles or whatever. We ate a lot of that. And there was a lot of wheatgrass around, which there wasn't so much over here in the UK. So we were like gunning wheatgrass all the time, trying to sort of stay awake.

Amazing. I think you called it more of a fact-finding mission on that tour. What were you finding out?

I guess whether people wanted us to come. I mean, you know, like I said, it's the only time we've been. So you never know whether people really want you to come or not. And yeah, and we were so well received at the gigs. Gigs were great. So we thought, oh, we do, you know, we do have an audience here that like us.

And for anyone coming to the final Saint Etienne shows happening at the Forum here in November in Melbourne, would you mind maybe sharing a little bit about what you've got planned for the farewell shows?

Yeah, so they're all, they're all a deep dive into all the old singles, all the fans' favourite songs. So again, they're mainly upbeat, dancey, party vibe. But yes, fan favourites and singles. And yeah, like I said, a couple of deep dive songs that we haven't played for so long, but we know the fans like them. I'm not going to tell you which ones, though, not yet. Surprise.

Well, yeah, we're very much looking forward to the Saint Etienne tour at the end of the year. And yeah, thank you so much for all of the incredible music and can't wait to see you in Australia in November. Thanks so much for joining me, Sarah.

Thank you. It's been fun. Thank you.
